title: Bright or Close? Luminosity
objective: After this level you can explain the difference between how bright a star looks and how bright it really is.
summary: A star’s apparent brightness depends on its luminosity and its distance, fading with the square of distance.

cards.headline: The brightest star in the sky isn’t the most powerful. It’s just close.
Two kinds of bright
cards.body: How bright a star looks from Earth depends on two things: how much light it really gives off, its luminosity, and how far away it is. A modest star nearby can outshine a powerhouse far away.

cards.headline: Fading with distance
cards.body: A star’s brightness falls with the square of its distance. Move a star twice as far away and it looks only a quarter as bright; ten times as far, a hundredth.
cards.callout: Twice as far → ¼ as bright

cards.fact: Sirius, the brightest night-time star, is about 8.6 light-years away.
cards.context: It’s more luminous than the Sun, and relatively close. Many far more powerful stars look fainter because they are much farther away.

cards.headline: Starlight: weighed
learned: Apparent brightness depends on luminosity and distance
Brightness falls with the square of distance
Sirius looks brightest partly because it’s close
Luminosity is a star’s true output

options.label: How bright it looks from Earth
How much light it actually gives off
How far away it is in light-years
How hot its surface is in degrees
options.rationale: Temperature is related, but luminosity is total output.

questions.explanation: Luminosity is a star’s true light output, regardless of distance.

questions.prompt: A star is moved to twice its distance. How bright does it look?
questions.explanation: Brightness falls with the square of distance: twice as far means 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 as bright.

questions.prompt: From Level 27: which other effect weakens with the square of distance, just like starlight?

options.label: The speed of light
options.rationale: Light’s speed doesn’t change with distance.

options.label: How fast a planet spins on its axis
options.rationale: Spin rate doesn’t depend on distance from anything.

questions.explanation: Newton’s gravity and starlight both spread out and weaken with the square of the distance.
